A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Generative Photomontage with the same authors and core method. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation results, quantitative baseline comparisons in Table 1, user surveys in Figure 10 and Appendix D, and qualitative ablations.

after.justification: V3 reports original quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–3, updated user surveys in Figure 8, and additional generated examples, including SDXL results in Appendix J.

M1.justification: The feature-space graph-cut objective and composite Q/K/V attention injection in Equations 1–6 are retained, including using the model-generated query for the base image. V3 tests the same procedure on SDXL with an adjusted parameter; it introduces no new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: V3 extends the illustrated domains to shoe and costume design, posters, and additional artistic compositions and shape-correction cases (Figures 13–19). The underlying tasks—appearance mixing, shape/artifact correction, and prompt alignment—and conditioning types remain the same. The SDXL addition concerns model settings rather than a new task.

E2.justification: The blending comparator set is retained: IDP, BLD, BLD+MultiDiffusion, MasaCtrl+ControlNet, CollageDiffusion, CDC, Deep Image Blending, GP-GAN, and appendix-only PCT-Net. SAM, alternative graph-cut features, and alternative attention-injection strategies were also evaluated in v1. V3 adds quantitative evidence for existing alternatives.

E3.justification: V3 specifies a 20-example evaluation and adds masked SSIM alongside the retained metrics. Across the same 12 survey scenes, completed realism/blending surveys increase from 16/10 to 27/20. Appendix J adds exploratory SDXL evaluation with sigma=25, compared with sigma=10 for SD1.5. The principal comparison design remains intact.

E4.justification: V3 adds a sigma sensitivity test at 1, 10, and 100 (Figure 10), quantitative attention-injection ablations (Table 2), and quantitative segmentation substitutions using SAM and IDP graph cut (Table 3). These extend v1's qualitative component comparisons; its existing feature, layer, timestep, and segmentation-boundary analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V3 Figure 8 adds error bars explicitly identified as standard errors. V1 Figure 10 reports vote counts without uncertainty bars. Neither version reports a repeated-seed uncertainty protocol for the automated image-quality metrics.

E6.justification: Table 1 contains revised aggregates: ours changes from LPIPS 0.104 and PSNR 23.44 to 0.123 and 22.46, and CollageDiffusion replaces BLD as the PSNR runner-up. Expanded example coverage prevents interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. V3 also adds SSIM results, Tables 2–3, SDXL outputs, and updated survey outcomes. Reported blending time changes from 7–13 seconds to about 3 seconds without matched workload descriptions.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, graph-cut costs, and attention-composition equations are unchanged. Neither version contains formal proofs or theorems. V3's parameter explanations and additional empirical metric do not introduce new formal reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding discussion retain the central contributions: user-guided compositing of generated images, diffusion-feature segmentation, and attention-based blending that preserves selected appearances. The additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretation of excessive or insufficient sigma values and tentatively attributes SDXL's different parameter requirement to its feature-map size and feature semantics. It also discusses the new SSIM findings alongside color fidelity. The curved-boundary and spatial-consistency limitations remain, relocated to Appendix I.

D1.justification: V3 adds a graph-cut runtime breakdown, including approximately 3 ms for the solver, VRAM and feature-regeneration guidance, and SDXL parameter information. Most baseline implementation details are retained and consolidated in Appendix F. Some specificity is lost: Appendix G omits v1's description of survey participants as computer science graduate students. The project-access link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds the SSIM reference and several image-source citations associated with new examples. The related-work categories and positioning relative to photomontage, image editing, and controllable generation remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The evaluation narrative is substantially reorganized: baseline-specific discussion is consolidated, segmentation and ablation subsections are reordered, and runtime details and limitations move into a reorganized appendix. The supplement expands from sections A–E to A–K. Introduction and method prose receive comparatively limited editing.

P2.justification: V3 substantially rearranges and condenses the main result figures while retaining fuller versions in the appendix. Table 1 is transposed and gains an SSIM column; Tables 2–3 and the sigma and SDXL figures are added. The survey plot gains percentage annotations and error bars, and numerous existing figures are relocated or regrouped.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens the existing empirical case through quantitative component ablations, larger surveys with uncertainty reporting, parameter sensitivity evidence, and initial SDXL demonstrations. These provide useful validation beyond v1's largely qualitative component analyses. The gains refine an already extensive evaluation; SDXL evidence remains limited to two examples. Omitting the earlier survey-cohort description is a small reporting loss, but the overall balance favors v3.
